query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a controlled amount of Cr in refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) can improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with varying compositions of Ti, Ta, and V
generation.intervention: Addition of a controlled amount of Cr
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (up to 900 °C) and mechanical loading
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Laves phases, such as TaCr2, and their composition, e.g., (Ti, Ta)(V, Cr)2
generation.mechanism: The Cr addition promotes the formation of Laves phases, which can enhance the mechanical behavior of the alloys at high temperatures
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature mechanical capability, limited density increase, and preserved room-temperature performance
generation.boundary: The optimal amount of Cr addition and the resulting phase composition
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Cr required to achieve the desired properties and the potential effects of other alloying elements on the phase formation and mechanical behavior

falsification_experiment.design: Mechanical testing of RHEAs with varying Cr content at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Cr does not result in improved high-temperature mechanical capability or leads to a significant increase in density, the hypothesis is falsified

The results indicate that Ti-oxide is a dominant second phase and is considerably dispersed in the BCC solid solution phase []. In addition, the high level of Cr encourages the formation of Laves phases, which change the mechanical behavior of the materials [,]. It should be also noted that phase stability of RHEAs can be influenced by annealing treatment. An increase in the number of C15 Laves phases can be obtained after the annealing of TiVZrMoW alloy []. Thus, in this work, four model RHEAs with a variation of Ti, Ta, and V have been designed and produced by mechanical alloying, namely, WVTaTi, WVTaTiCr, WV10Ta10TiCr, and WVTaTi5Cr. This study aims to understand the effects of alloying elements and mechanical alloying on the formation of second phases, microstructure evolution, and mechanical behavior of the WVTaTiCr model alloys. The phase formation of the milled powders and sintered RHEAs was characterized by an X’Pert PRO X-ray diffractometer (XRD, PANalytical, Almelo, The Netherlands) equipped with a copper target. The diffracted intensity of KαCu radiation was measured in the 2θ range from 30° to 110° at a scanning rate of 4° min−1. Microstructure development and chemical analysis of the model RHEAs were examined by a Hitachi-4700 scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi High-Tech Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK). The phase transformation and the crystal structure of different phases were determined using a FEI Tecnai F20 G2 Field Emission Gun TEM (FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR, USA). ImageJ software (V1.53) was used to manually measure the particle size of the model RHEAs. Vickers hardness tests were performed using a load of 9.8 N for a holding time of 15 s at room temperature.

The presented data sheet is a compilation of essential data on RHEAs and RCCAs. All RHEAs and RCCAs reported in the literature through the end of January 2018 crystallize with at least one phase with body centered cubic (BCC) structure.
